chip-capabilities.title: What the FDO2 does
chip-capabilities.alt: Capability map of the FDO2: Oxygen and temperature (supported): Measures the oxygen partial pressure and the temperature, as hPa or as a volume fraction; Raw values and housing sensors (supported): Adds the phase shift, signal and ambient light, and the pressure and humidity inside the housing; Status word (supported): Classifies each reading's warning and fatal bits and holds back a faulty measurement; Identity and start-up (supported): Waits out the power-up, reads the version and the unique ID, and flashes the status LED to find a module; Calibration (guarded): Calibrates at zero oxygen, at a known partial pressure or in dry air; the factory calibration is lost; Broadcast stream (guarded): Makes the module measure by itself at a set interval and send each result; Measurement mode, CRC and baud rate (guarded): Trades drift for noise, adds a CRC-16 to every reply, and changes the baud rate; User memory (guarded): Reads and writes 64 words that survive a power cycle; each write costs a flash cycle.
chip-capabilities.description: Each card is one function of the FDO2: an icon, its name and what it does for the application. The filled pill says how this driver covers it (legend below); the outlined pills are the chip registers behind it. The coverage table in the README gives the driver calls and the datasheet section of each card.

chip-hero.title: FDO2
chip-hero.alt: Overview of the FDO2, an optical oxygen sensor module with a UART: it excites a sensor dye with red light, measures the luminescence that oxygen quenches, and reports the oxygen partial pressure with its temperature, compensated and factory calibrated. A MCU talks to it over UART, 3.0 V; it reads back Oxygen, Temperature, pressure, humidity. Headline figures: 0 to 1000 hPa typical oxygen partial pressure range; < 2 s response time (t63); 3.3 to 5.0 V supply; 19200 baud UART at power-up, 8N1, 3.0 V.
chip-hero.description: The FDO2 in the middle, drawn as its Module, 4-pin package. On the left the MCU that runs the driver, joined to it by UART, 3.0 V. Below it, what the chip reads back. The tiles at the bottom are the headline numbers, each with the datasheet section and page it comes from.

driver-layers.title: The layers, one of them yours
driver-layers.alt: Layer diagram: your application calls the FDO2 core, which sends register reads and writes through the UART port contract to the port class you write, which drives the chip; the core and the contract are the same on every MCU.
driver-layers.description: Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers.

one-call-through-the-layers.title: One call through the layers
one-call-through-the-layers.alt: One call through the layers: your code calls MeasureOxygen(), the core exchanges frames with the chip through your port and returns the result to your code.
one-call-through-the-layers.description: Participants, left to right: Your code, FDO2<Port> and Your port. The steps run from top to bottom. Your code sends MeasureOxygen() to FDO2<Port>. FDO2<Port> sends FlushInput() to Your port. FDO2<Port> sends Write("#MOXY") to Your port. A note over FDO2<Port> and Your port says: Repeat until CR or deadline. FDO2<Port> sends Read(buffer, max, timeout) to Your port. Your port returns n bytes to FDO2<Port>. A note over FDO2<Port> and Your port says: End of the repeated steps. A note over FDO2<Port> says: assemble the line, check CRC, parse. A note over FDO2<Port> says: status policy, plausibility windows. FDO2<Port> returns Result<Oxygen> to Your code.

state-machine.title: The driver's states
state-machine.alt: State diagram of fdo2::FDO2: Uninitialized, PoweringUp, Idle, Waiting, Streaming, Draining and StateUnknown, with the calls and events that move between them.
state-machine.description: Each box is a State of fdo2::FDO2, read from the enumeration in inc/fdo2_types.hpp; each arrow is a call or an event that moves it. Start-up goes through PoweringUp to Idle. An operation (Start* or a blocking call) puts the driver in Waiting; a good reply returns it to Idle. A timeout, a CRC error or a refused line sends it through Draining, where input is discarded until the line is quiet, so a late reply is never read as the next answer. A flash-writing command or a baud change that ended without a confirmed echo leaves StateUnknown, which only Resync() or a power cycle ends. While the module streams, Idle is reported as Streaming. The transitions are fixed in this figure and checked against the names used in src/fdo2.ipp.

transaction-timing.title: One command and its reply
transaction-timing.alt: Five steps of a transaction: flush the receive buffer, write the command, wait for the module, read the echo and values, end at the carriage return; the allowance of each kind of command is listed under the wait.
transaction-timing.description: A transaction is five steps, left to right. The driver drops what is in the receive buffer, writes the command and its carriage return, then waits for the module: the module echoes the command, with its values, and ends the reply with one carriage return. The wait is the characters' airtime at the current baud rate, plus the module's processing allowance for the command (command_ms, measurement_ms, calibration_ms, flash_ms or logo_ms of the Config), plus margin_ms. The numbers shown are the Config defaults, read from inc/fdo2_types.hpp. A reply that does not end in time is a Timeout: the driver drains the line, and sends an idempotent read again when retries allow.
